title: GrowthOptix
summary: Backend engineering on a marketing-attribution platform: advertising and payment integrations, event-driven ingestion, identity resolution and the analytics APIs behind cross-platform reporting.
context:
The platform unified advertising, payment and lifecycle data into attribution and reporting workflows for marketing teams. The engineering difficulty was not any single integration: it was the number of sources that describe the same customer differently, and the requirement that a report be defensible across all of them.

The ecosystem also included Gox Analytics, a user-behavior analytics service built around a tracking script and an event API. Its event model carries a user and session identifier, the event name and timestamp, and contextual metadata such as URL, referrer, device and browser. Aggregations cover referrers, landing pages, device and geography, plus session and behavior metrics.

solution.title: Advertising integrations end to end
solution.body: Google Ads, Meta Ads, Microsoft Advertising and LinkedIn Ads integrations, including OAuth token lifecycle, synchronisation jobs and the REST and GraphQL surfaces that expose the collected data.

solution.title: Event-driven ingestion
solution.body: Pipelines on BullMQ, RabbitMQ and Amazon SQS process tracking events for several attribution models, with webhook ingestion for Calendly, Stripe, PayPal, Typeform and ThriveCart feeding the same flow.

solution.title: Attribution that keeps the source visible
solution.body: Meta's 7-day post-click attribution was stored as parallel fields in BigQuery, with a feature flag controlling whether the frontend shows it. Platform-reported attribution and the system's own first-party events stay distinguishable instead of overwriting each other.

solution.title: Identity resolution
solution.body: A resolution engine scores identity matches across touchpoints so a new device can be connected to a known contact, while a low-confidence match is refused rather than merging two people into one.

solution.title: Reporting without double counting
solution.body: Cross-platform reconciliation and a contact-profile read path moved from MongoDB to BigQuery, so the analytics API answers profile queries from the store built for that shape of data.

contribution: As a Mid Backend Developer I worked on the backend integrations, event pipelines, analytics APIs, webhook ingestion, identity-resolution workflows and cross-platform reconciliation. Within that work I contributed to the Gox Analytics event API and its aggregations (referrer, landing page, device, geography), the Google Ads, Meta Ads and Microsoft Advertising integrations, and the 7-day post-click attribution work in BigQuery. The platform was a team effort: I do not claim authorship of every component, and platform figures remain unpublished until they are validated.
approach:
The consistent theme was making two sources agree before making them fast. A dashboard on top of double-counted data is worse than no dashboard: it is confidently wrong. Reconciliation came first, then the read path — moving contact-profile reads to BigQuery was worthwhile because the query had already been reshaped to ask a narrower question.

Attribution adds a second kind of disagreement: what the advertising platform reports versus what the product actually observed. Keeping both, instead of replacing one with the other, is what lets a report explain a difference instead of hiding it.

On the integration side, the work that decides whether something survives its second month is rarely the happy path. Token refresh, retries, idempotency and the failure that arrives twice are the actual deliverable.

technicalDecisions.title: Reshape the query, then move the read path
technicalDecisions.body: Contact-profile reads were served from MongoDB, where the query shape fought the document model. Narrowing the question and serving it from BigQuery turned an expensive scan into a lookup. The CV reports a large latency reduction; the measurement conditions are not documented, so no figure is published here.

technicalDecisions.title: Keep platform-reported and first-party attribution separate
technicalDecisions.body: Storing 7-day post-click attribution as parallel fields, behind a feature flag, keeps Meta's reported view distinguishable from the events the product recorded. Overwriting one with the other would make every later comparison meaningless.

technicalDecisions.title: Confidence scoring before merging identities
technicalDecisions.body: Attribution improves when more touchpoints are connected, and a false merge is much worse than an unmatched event: it attributes one person's revenue to another. Scoring the match and refusing the weak ones keeps the engine honest.

technicalDecisions.title: One pipeline behind several event sources
technicalDecisions.body: Webhooks from five providers normalize into one attribution flow instead of five bespoke paths. The cost is a shared contract that must be maintained; the gain is that reconciliation and reporting are written once.

outcomes: Advertising integrations cover Google Ads, Meta Ads, Microsoft Advertising and LinkedIn Ads, with OAuth token lifecycle handled in the backend.
Webhook ingestion for Calendly, Stripe, PayPal, Typeform and ThriveCart feeds one attribution pipeline.
Identity resolution scores matches and refuses low-confidence merges.
Cross-platform reconciliation removed double counting between sources.
Contact-profile reads moved from MongoDB to a reshaped BigQuery query.
Behavior analytics covers referrers, landing pages, devices, geography and session metrics.
